_comment: Weird-fact cards: one unlocks when a skill reaches MASTERED. Museum collectibles.

facts.title: The Golden Purr
facts.text: Sunflower seeds, pinecones, and galaxy spirals all follow ratios from the Fibonacci sequence — nature keeps using the same recipe card.

facts.title: Percent = Per Centum
facts.text: 'Percent' is Latin for 'per hundred' — Roman tax collectors charged 1/100 on goods sold at auction, the centesima rerum venalium.

facts.title: The Decimal Point Was Shy
facts.text: Europeans wrote decimals at least four different ways for 100+ years — 2|35, 2(35), 2,35 — before the humble dot mostly won.

facts.title: The Nightingale Chart
facts.text: Florence Nightingale invented rose diagrams to convince generals that soldiers were dying of bad hospitals, not battles — a graph literally saved lives.

facts.title: Born at a Gambling Table
facts.text: Probability theory began when two mathematicians, Pascal and Fermat, exchanged letters about how to fairly split the pot of an unfinished dice game.

facts.title: π Has No Final Digit
facts.text: π's digits never end and never repeat. People have computed over 100 trillion of them — yet 39 digits are enough to measure the universe to within one atom.

facts.title: The Alligator Is Older Than You Think
facts.text: The symbols < and > first appeared in print in 1631, in a book published ten years after its author Thomas Harriot died.

facts.title: The Fly on the Ceiling
facts.text: Legend says Descartes invented coordinates while watching a fly walk on his ceiling — every position just two numbers away.

facts.title: Double a Penny
facts.text: A penny doubled every day is worth over $5 million after 30 days — exponential growth starts as a whisper and ends as a roar.

facts.title: Why x?
facts.text: One theory: Spanish printers had no letter for the Arabic 'shay' (thing), so they borrowed the Greek chi — and x became math's favorite mystery.

facts.title: Al-Jabr
facts.text: 'Algebra' comes from al-jabr — 'the reunion of broken parts' — from al-Khwarizmi's 9th-century book on balancing equations.

facts.title: The Eye of Horus
facts.text: Ancient Egyptians wrote fractions using parts of the Eye of Horus symbol — 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 — each piece of the eye a different unit fraction.

facts.title: Primes Guard Your Secrets
facts.text: Every time you shop online, giant prime numbers encrypt your data — multiplying primes is easy, un-multiplying them is nearly impossible.

facts.title: Negative Numbers Were Illegal-ish
facts.text: European mathematicians called negative numbers 'absurd' for centuries — while Chinese mathematicians had been computing with red and black rods since 200 BCE.

facts.title: Battleship Is Just Math
facts.text: Every game of Battleship, every pixel on this screen, and every GPS location is the coordinate plane wearing a costume.

facts.title: The 4,000-Year-Old Word Problem
facts.text: Babylonian clay tablets from 1800 BCE contain word problems almost identical to yours — students have been asking 'when will the trains meet' for four millennia.

facts.title: Venn's Actual Diagrams
facts.text: John Venn drew his famous circles in 1880 — and his college installed a stained-glass window of them, the nerdiest window in Cambridge.

facts.title: The Wolf River
facts.text: When wolves returned to Yellowstone, rivers changed shape — fewer elk meant more trees, more beavers, steadier banks. Food webs can bend geography.

facts.title: Space Is Silent, Mostly
facts.text: Sound can't cross empty space — but a black hole 250 million light-years away hums a B-flat 57 octaves below middle C through the gas around it.

facts.title: Dinosaur Water
facts.text: Earth barely gains or loses water — the glass you drank today almost certainly contains molecules that once passed through a dinosaur.

facts.title: The $125 Million Typo
facts.text: NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one team used metric units and another used imperial — units aren't decoration, they're survival.

facts.title: You Are Stardust, Literally
facts.text: Almost every atom in you heavier than hydrogen was forged inside a star that exploded before the Sun was born.

facts.title: The Comma That Cost $5 Million
facts.text: Maine dairy drivers won a $5 million lawsuit because a law was missing one Oxford comma — punctuation with a paycheck.

facts.title: Nice Used To Mean Silly
facts.text: 'Nice' meant 'foolish' in the 1300s, then 'precise,' then 'pleasant' — words molt their meanings like butterflies.

facts.title: The Hero's 1,000 Faces
facts.text: Myth-scholars found the same story shape — call to adventure, trials, return — in heroes from Gilgamesh to modern wizards. Plots rhyme across millennia.

facts.title: Reading Rewires You
facts.text: Brain scans show that reading about an action lights up some of the same regions as doing it — every novel is a flight simulator for being someone else.

facts.title: Drafts of Genius
facts.text: Famous authors routinely rewrote openings dozens of times — a 'gifted' first sentence is usually the twentieth attempt in a trench coat.

facts.title: Cheek-Kiss Mathematics
facts.text: La bise (greeting kisses) varies by region of France — one, two, three, even four kisses. There are maps. The maps disagree.

facts.title: Eighty = Four Twenties
facts.text: French quatre-vingts (4×20) is a leftover from Celtic counting by twenties — Belgium and Switzerland gave up and say 'octante/huitante'.

facts.title: The Revolution Renamed Time
facts.text: Revolutionary France ran a calendar with 10-day weeks and months named Fog, Snow, and Harvest — it lasted 12 chaotic years.

facts.title: Grand-père Is Literally Big Father
facts.text: French builds family words like Lego: grand (big) + père (father). English borrowed the same trick — 'grandfather' is a French import.

facts.title: Wednesday Was Freedom
facts.text: Many French elementary schools traditionally had Wednesdays (or afternoons) off — and some still split the difference. Les devoirs find you anyway.

facts.title: Why Orange Breaks the Rules
facts.text: 'Orange' won't agree with nouns because it's secretly a fruit moonlighting as an adjective — French treats it as 'the color of an orange'.

facts.title: The Croissant Isn't French
facts.text: The croissant descends from Vienna's kipferl — Austrian bakers brought it to Paris, where French butter and folding made it legendary.

facts.title: Le Weekend Wars
facts.text: The Académie française has battled English loanwords like 'le weekend' for decades — the French public cheerfully keeps using them.

facts.title: Noon Cannons
facts.text: The Palais-Royal garden in Paris has a tiny cannon that once fired itself at exact noon, lit by a magnifying lens focusing the sun.

facts.title: The Cat Owns the House
facts.text: French has a saying: 'À bon chat, bon rat' — and any French cat owner will confirm the chat considers every chambre theirs.

facts.title: The Man Who Broke Gold
facts.text: Mansa Musa gave away so much gold passing through Cairo in 1324 that gold's value there reportedly stayed depressed for years — one traveler crashed a market.

facts.title: The Most Valuable Invention Is Nothing
facts.text: Indian mathematicians made zero a true number — Brahmagupta wrote its rules in 628 CE. Every 0 in your code and bank balance traces back there.

facts.title: Ships That Dwarfed Columbus
facts.text: Zheng He's largest treasure ships may have been 4–5 times the length of the Santa María — with crews of hundreds and cats aboard for pest control.

facts.title: Books on Chains
facts.text: Hand-copied books were so precious that medieval libraries chained them to the shelves — a single Bible could cost as much as a house.

facts.title: Mirror-Writing Genius
facts.text: Leonardo da Vinci wrote his notebooks right-to-left in mirror script — readable only with a mirror, possibly just because he was left-handed and hated smudges.

facts.title: The Tomato Is an Immigrant
facts.text: Italy had NO tomatoes until the Columbian Exchange — pizza margherita, ketchup, and salsa all depend on a plant from the Americas.
